lessons.title: Suspecting and working up endometriosis without waiting for laparoscopy
lessons.objective: Recognise the symptoms that should raise endometriosis and the diagnostic delay, know the limits of examination, combine work-up with empirical treatment, know when to refer and adapt the approach to adolescents.
lessons.closing: Suspect it from a cluster of symptoms, examine knowing examination misses disease, treat while investigating and refer according to findings: gynaecology service or specialist centre.

lessons.title: Treating pain: analgesics, hormones and surgery
lessons.objective: Sequence the treatment of endometriosis-associated pain: analgesics, first-line hormones, GnRH agonists and antagonists with add-back, aromatase inhibitors for refractory pain, and the role of surgery and recurrence prevention, noting where ESHRE and NICE differ.
lessons.closing: Analgesics with a review date, combined contraceptive or progestogen as first line, GnRH agonists or antagonists as second line (with add-back for agonists) and, after surgery, long-term hormonal suppression if she is not seeking pregnancy.

lessons.title: Diet, supplements and complementary therapies: what the guidelines say
lessons.objective: Explain honestly what ESHRE and NICE conclude on nutrition, supplements, acupuncture, TENS, physiotherapy, exercise and psychological interventions for endometriosis-associated pain, and how to integrate psychological and multidisciplinary support.
lessons.closing: No specific non-medical intervention is supported for pain; they are discussed without promises, without replacing effective treatments, and with psychological and multidisciplinary support at hand.

items.title: Symptoms that should raise endometriosis, and diagnostic delay
items.core: ESHRE recommends considering endometriosis in people with cyclical or non-cyclical signs and symptoms: dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dysuria, dyschezia, painful rectal bleeding or haematuria, shoulder tip pain, catamenial pneumothorax, cyclical cough, haemoptysis or chest pain, cyclical scar swelling and pain, fatigue and infertility (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE asks clinicians to suspect it, including in young women aged 17 and under, with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea affecting daily life, deep pain during or after intercourse, cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms (particularly painful bowel movements, blood in the urine or pain passing urine), or infertility together with any of these (1.3.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
NICE describes delays of 4 to 10 years between first reporting symptoms and confirming the diagnosis; patient self-help groups emphasise that clinicians often do not recognise the importance of the symptoms, and women may delay seeking help because they perceive pelvic pain as normal. [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] ESHRE notes that the ability of symptoms alone to predict the disease is weak and incomplete; in a UK primary care database, the likelihood of diagnosis rose with the number of symptoms (OR 5.0 with 1 symptom and 84.7 with 7). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

NICE asks about endometriosis in first-degree relatives, because it increases the likelihood (1.3.2), and advises telling women that a pain and symptom diary can aid discussions (1.3.3). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] ESHRE acknowledges there is no evidence that a diary, questionnaire or app shortens time to diagnosis, but considers that they complement history taking because they help objectify pain (GDG statement). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: Which cyclical extrapelvic symptoms does ESHRE list among those that should raise endometriosis?
items.pearl: No single symptom confirms or rules out endometriosis: the more compatible symptoms, the more likely it is.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 1: GPP; symptom diary: GDG statement (ungraded). On ESHRE’s GRADE scale, ⊕ = very low evidence, ⊕⊕ = low, ⊕⊕⊕ = moderate and ⊕⊕⊕⊕ = high; strength (strong/weak) and quality of evidence are different things. NICE NG73 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 [2017]; 1.3.2 [2024]. The 4–10-year figure comes from the NICE guideline’s context section, not from a recommendation.

items.title: Clinical examination: useful, but of limited accuracy
items.core: ESHRE recommends considering clinical examination, including vaginal examination where appropriate, to identify deep nodules or endometriomas, although its diagnostic accuracy is low (strong, ⊕), and proceeding to further steps such as imaging even if the examination is normal (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE offers abdominal and pelvic examination to identify masses and signs such as reduced organ mobility and enlargement, tender nodularity in the posterior vaginal fornix and visible vaginal lesions (1.3.5). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
In a prospective study of 129 women summarised by ESHRE, the sensitivity and specificity of examination were 44% and 99% for the ovary, 50% and 80% for the uterosacral ligaments, 76% and 92% for the pouch of Douglas, 25% and 100% for the bladder, and 39% and 97% for the rectosigmoid; transvaginal ultrasound was superior for the ovary, uterosacral ligaments and rectosigmoid. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Another prospective study showed that examination is more reliable during menstruation. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

ESHRE concludes that examination does not reliably predict the disease and points out that vaginal or rectovaginal examination may be inappropriate or very painful (for example in adolescents, for religious reasons or after sexual abuse); in those cases it should ideally be omitted and other techniques used first. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] If pelvic examination is declined or not suitable, NICE offers an abdominal examination to exclude masses (1.3.6). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE recommend if the pelvic examination of a woman with suspected endometriosis is normal?
items.pearl: A normal examination does not close the work-up: ESHRE recommends going on to imaging anyway.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 2: strong, ⊕; rec. 3: strong, ⊕⊕ (its evidence level derives from the imaging studies). NICE NG73 1.3.5 and 1.3.6 [2017, amended 2024].

items.title: Treating while investigating: empirical treatment or laparoscopy
items.core: ESHRE considers both diagnostic laparoscopy and imaging combined with empirical treatment (hormonal contraceptives or progestogens) valid options, with no proven superiority of either, and asks for pros and cons to be discussed with the patient (GDG statement). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE advises carrying out ultrasound and, if needed, referral in parallel with initial pharmacological treatment (1.5.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
ESHRE notes that, although there are no adequate studies on the benefit of earlier versus later diagnosis, attempts should be made to relieve symptoms in symptomatic women, either by empirical treatment or after a diagnosis (GDG statement). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] It also questions the “dogma” of laparoscopy as the gold standard, since it is an invasive procedure with potential morbidity, and suggests offering it for diagnosis and treatment if imaging is negative or empirical treatment was unsuccessful or inappropriate (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

NICE, in its context section, still describes laparoscopic visualisation as the only route to a definitive diagnosis; it recommends considering laparoscopy even if ultrasound or MRI was normal (1.5.11) and, if deep disease is suspected, a specialist ultrasound or MRI before operative laparoscopy (1.5.12). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] It also asks that treatment be guided by the woman’s symptoms, preferences and priorities rather than by stage (1.6.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: According to NICE, should pharmacological treatment wait for the ultrasound or the referral?
items.pearl: Endometriosis does not need to be confirmed before starting pain relief: work-up and treatment run in parallel.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: GDG statements (ungraded); rec. 6: GPP. NICE NG73 1.5.1 [2024]; 1.5.11 and 1.5.12 [2017, amended 2024]; 1.6.1 [2017]. Difference in emphasis: ESHRE questions laparoscopy as the gold standard; the NICE context section still presents it as the only route to a definitive diagnosis.

items.title: When to refer: gynaecology service or specialist centre
items.core: NICE refers to a gynaecology service if initial treatment is not effective, not tolerated or contraindicated, if symptoms affect daily living, if they persist or recur, or if there are pelvic signs without suspected deep disease (1.5.5). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] It refers to a specialist endometriosis service for suspected or confirmed endometrioma, deep endometriosis (including bowel, bladder or ureter involvement) or endometriosis outside the pelvic cavity (1.5.6). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] ESHRE recommends referring women with deep endometriosis to a centre of expertise (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
For NICE, the specialist centre should have access to gynaecologists with advanced laparoscopic skills, a colorectal surgeon and a urologist with an interest in endometriosis, a specialist nurse, a multidisciplinary pain management service with expertise in pelvic pain, a professional with specialist expertise in gynaecological imaging of endometriosis, advanced diagnostic facilities and fertility services (1.1.4). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

On follow-up, NICE suggests considering outpatient review, with or without examination and imaging, particularly for women who choose not to have surgery, when there is deep endometriosis of the bowel, bladder or ureter or 1 or more endometriomas larger than 3 cm (1.7.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] ESHRE suggests considering follow-up and psychological support in confirmed endometriosis, particularly deep and ovarian disease (weak, ⊕), although there is no evidence that regular monitoring detects recurrence, complications or malignancy earlier, and asks for its frequency to be individualised (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: Which three findings lead NICE to refer to a specialist endometriosis service?
items.pearl: Endometrioma, deep or extrapelvic disease: specialist centre. Pain that does not respond, limits daily life, persists or recurs: gynaecology service.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG73 1.5.5 and 1.5.6 [2017, amended 2024]; 1.1.4 and 1.7.1 [2017]. ESHRE 2022, rec. 30: GPP; rec. 8: weak, ⊕; rec. 9: GPP.

items.title: Adolescents: clues in daily life and first-line hormonal treatment
items.core: In adolescents, ESHRE recommends careful history taking for risk factors (family history, obstructive genital malformations, early menarche or short cycles) (strong, ⊕) and considering endometriosis with (cyclical) school absenteeism or use of oral contraceptives for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] It recommends transvaginal ultrasound where appropriate and, if not, considering MRI or transabdominal, transperineal or transrectal ultrasound (strong, ⊕⊕), and not using serum biomarkers such as CA-125 to diagnose or rule it out (strong, ⊕⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE refers young women aged 17 and under with suspected or confirmed endometriosis to a paediatric and adolescent gynaecology service or a specialist centre (1.5.7). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
Before vaginal or rectal examination, ESHRE asks for its acceptability to be discussed with the adolescent and her caregiver, taking age and cultural background into account (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] As first-line hormonal therapy it recommends hormonal contraceptives or progestogens (systemic or via levonorgestrel IUS), noting that some progestogens may decrease bone mineral density (strong, ⊕), and suggests considering NSAIDs, especially if first-line hormonal treatment is not an option (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Diagnostic laparoscopy may be considered if imaging is negative and NSAIDs or contraceptives have failed (weak, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

GnRH agonists are reserved for laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis after hormonal contraceptives or progestogens have failed, for up to 1 year and with add-back (weak, ⊕⊕), and only after careful discussion with a practitioner in secondary or tertiary care (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: Which two everyday situations in an adolescent does ESHRE suggest as clues to endometriosis?
items.pearl: Missing school every month because of periods, or taking the pill for dysmenorrhoea, are clues, not normality.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 70 (strong, ⊕), 71 (weak, ⊕), 73 (GPP), 74 (strong, ⊕⊕), 75 (strong, ⊕⊕⊕), 76 (weak, ⊕⊕), 78 (strong, ⊕), 79 and 81 (GPP), 80 (weak, ⊕⊕). NICE NG73 1.5.7 [2017, amended 2024].

items.stem: According to ESHRE, which of these presentations should prompt consideration of endometriosis?

options.text: Shoulder tip pain that appears with menstruation.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE includes shoulder tip pain, together with other cyclical extrapelvic symptoms such as catamenial pneumothorax, among those that should prompt consideration of endometriosis.

options.text: Only severe dysmenorrhoea; other symptoms are not informative.
options.why: ESHRE also includes deep dyspareunia, dysuria, dyschezia, cyclical extrapelvic symptoms, fatigue and infertility, and in primary care the likelihood rose with the number of symptoms.

options.text: A raised CA125 on routine blood tests.
options.why: ESHRE recommends against using biomarkers to diagnose endometriosis (strong, ⊕⊕⊕) and NICE advises not to use CA125 for that purpose (1.5.8).

options.text: Pelvic pain only if strictly cyclical; non-cyclical pain rules it out.
options.why: ESHRE refers to cyclical and non-cyclical symptoms, and NICE includes chronic pelvic pain among the reasons for suspicion (1.3.1).

items.explanation: Suspicion rests on a broad set of pelvic and extrapelvic symptoms, cyclical or not; biomarkers do not diagnose it.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman (fictional case) with severe dysmenorrhoea and dyschezia, who does not want to become pregnant, has a normal pelvic examination and transvaginal ultrasound. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Explain that endometriosis has been ruled out and treat it as primary dysmenorrhoea.
options.why: NICE asks not to exclude endometriosis when examination and ultrasound are normal (1.5.4), and ESHRE points out that negative imaging does not exclude it, particularly superficial peritoneal disease.

options.text: Offer analgesia and empirical hormonal treatment (for example, a combined contraceptive), also discussing the option of laparoscopy.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE considers imaging plus empirical treatment and laparoscopy both valid, with neither superior, and NICE offers hormonal treatment for suspected endometriosis (1.4.6).

options.text: Start no treatment until the diagnosis is confirmed at laparoscopy.
options.why: ESHRE asks for symptoms to be relieved by empirical treatment or after diagnosis, and NICE runs the work-up in parallel with initial treatment (1.5.1).

options.text: Order CA125 to decide whether to continue the work-up.
options.why: NICE advises not to use CA125 to diagnose endometriosis (1.5.8) and ESHRE recommends against biomarkers (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

items.explanation: Normal imaging does not exclude endometriosis; if she is not seeking pregnancy, empirical treatment is a legitimate route, discussing its pros and cons against laparoscopy.

items.stem: According to NICE, which of these situations justifies referral to a specialist endometriosis service rather than only to a gynaecology service?

options.text: Pain persisting after 3 months of NSAIDs, with no signs of deep disease.
options.why: NICE refers this to a gynaecology service because initial treatment is not effective (1.5.5), not necessarily to a specialist centre.

options.text: Ultrasound suggesting a deep nodule involving the rectum.
options.why: Correct: suspected deep disease, including bowel involvement, is a reason for referral to a specialist centre (1.5.6), and ESHRE also recommends a centre of expertise (GPP).

options.text: Symptoms returning after hormonal treatment that had worked.
options.why: In NICE, persistent or recurrent symptoms lead to a gynaecology service (1.5.5).

options.text: Pelvic signs of endometriosis without suspected deep disease.
options.why: NICE lists this among the reasons for referral to gynaecology, not to the specialist centre (1.5.5).

items.explanation: Gynaecology for pain that does not respond, limits daily life, persists or recurs; specialist centre for endometrioma, deep or extrapelvic disease.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl (fictional case) misses 2 days of school every month because of severe dysmenorrhoea that does not respond to ibuprofen. Her mother has endometriosis and she has never had sexual intercourse. Which approach fits ESHRE?

options.text: Mandatory vaginal examination and transvaginal ultrasound before any treatment.
options.why: ESHRE asks for the acceptability of examination to be discussed first with the adolescent and her caregiver (GPP) and, if transvaginal ultrasound is not appropriate, for MRI or transabdominal, transperineal or transrectal ultrasound to be considered (strong, ⊕⊕).

options.text: Offer a hormonal contraceptive or a progestogen as first-line hormonal therapy, with imaging suited to her situation.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE recommends hormonal contraceptives or progestogens as first-line hormonal therapy in adolescents (strong, ⊕) and asks for risk factors such as family history to be recorded (strong, ⊕).

options.text: Start a GnRH agonist for 1 year with add-back.
options.why: ESHRE reserves it for laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis after contraceptives or progestogens have failed (weak, ⊕⊕), and after assessment in secondary or tertiary care (GPP).

options.text: Order CA-125 to decide whether it is endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend serum biomarkers such as CA-125 to diagnose or rule out endometriosis in adolescents (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

items.explanation: In adolescents, cyclical absenteeism and family history are clues; first-line hormonal treatment, adapted imaging and no biomarkers. NICE also refers young women aged 17 and under to paediatric and adolescent gynaecology or a specialist centre (1.5.7).

items.title: Analgesics and NSAIDs: a first step with scarce evidence
items.core: ESHRE states that NSAIDs or other analgesics may be offered, alone or with other treatments, to reduce pain (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE suggests considering a short trial (for example, 3 months) of paracetamol or an NSAID, alone or in combination, as first-line management (1.4.2) and, if relief is inadequate, considering other forms of pain management and referral for further assessment (1.4.3). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
ESHRE notes that the evidence for NSAIDs in endometriosis is limited to one small, very-low-quality trial, that there is no evidence that analgesics affect disease progression, and that NSAIDs can have gastrointestinal side effects. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] There is some limited evidence that NSAIDs taken continuously through the cycle might inhibit ovulation, which matters if pregnancy is sought. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Neuromodulators (tricyclic antidepressants, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin) are used for chronic pain, but in chronic pelvic pain trials they have not been shown to be clearly superior to placebo and sometimes cause severe, dose-limiting side effects. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE refers to its neuropathic pain guideline for their use (1.4.4). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: How long, as an example, is the paracetamol or NSAID trial NICE suggests, and what should happen if it does not work?
items.pearl: The NICE analgesic trial has a time frame: if it has not given enough relief after about 3 months, rethink and consider referral.

items.title: Combined contraceptives and progestogens: first-line hormonal treatment
items.core: ESHRE recommends offering hormone treatment (combined hormonal contraceptives, progestogens, GnRH agonists or antagonists) as one of the options to reduce pain (strong, ⊕⊕⊕), chosen through shared decision-making based on preferences, side effects, individual efficacy, cost and availability (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE offers hormonal treatment, for example the combined pill or a progestogen, for suspected, confirmed or recurrent endometriosis (1.4.6), and explains that it reduces pain and has no permanent negative effect on subsequent fertility (1.4.5). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
For ESHRE, all hormone treatments reduce pain compared with placebo by a similar magnitude, none is free of side effects, and differences between them in their capacity to reduce pain appear small; in practice, finding the right one is often trial and error. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] It recommends the combined hormonal contraceptive as a pill, vaginal ring or patch for dyspareunia, dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pain (strong, ⊕⊕), and allows the combined pill to be offered continuously for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕⊕), discussing possible breakthrough bleeding. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

It also recommends progestogens (strong, ⊕⊕), taking their different side-effect profiles into account (GPP), and the levonorgestrel IUS or etonogestrel implant (strong, ⊕⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] The long-term dienogest studies summarised by ESHRE used 2 mg/day, and in one of them vaginal bleeding was the most frequent side effect (71.9%). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] ESHRE no longer includes danazol among the treatments because of its severe side effects. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: Which hormone treatments does ESHRE recommend for pain, and which one may be used continuously for dysmenorrhoea?
items.pearl: In trials, hormone treatments reduce pain by a similar magnitude: side-effect profile, need for contraception and preference decide.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 11: strong, ⊕⊕⊕; rec. 12 and 16: GPP; rec. 13 and 15: strong, ⊕⊕; rec. 14: weak, ⊕⊕; rec. 17: strong, ⊕⊕⊕. NICE NG73 1.4.5 and 1.4.6 [2017] (in 2017, off-label use for some pills and progestogens).

items.title: GnRH agonists and antagonists: second line, with add-back
items.core: ESHRE recommends GnRH agonists to reduce pain (strong, ⊕⊕), as second line because of their side effects, for example if contraceptives or progestogens have failed (GPP), and considering combined hormonal add-back to prevent bone loss and hypoestrogenic symptoms (strong, ⊕⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Oral GnRH antagonists can be considered (weak, ⊕⊕⊕), also as second line (GPP), with limited evidence on dose, duration and need for add-back. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
In the Cochrane review summarised by ESHRE, agonists were more effective than placebo but inferior to the levonorgestrel IUS or oral danazol, with no difference by route of administration; their most frequent side effects were vaginal dryness, hot flushes, headache, weight gain and acne. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] A meta-analysis of 13 trials showed that add-back improves lumbar spine bone mineral density with no significant difference in dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] In the elagolix trials, more than 70% of women in each group reported an adverse event, more often with the higher dose than with placebo; the most common were hot flushes, headache and nausea. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

In NICE NG73, agonists appear only as an adjunct before surgery for deep disease (1.9.5). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] For antagonists, NICE points to its technology appraisals in adults of reproductive age after medical or surgical treatment: linzagolix with hormonal add-back (TA1067, June 2025) and relugolix–estradiol–norethisterone (TA1057, April 2025) (1.4.7 and 1.9.8). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Where in the treatment sequence does ESHRE place GnRH agonists and antagonists, and what does it add to agonists?
items.application: In Spain, relugolix with estradiol and norethisterone acetate (Ryeqo) and linzagolix (Yselty) are authorised and marketed for symptomatic endometriosis after previous medical or surgical treatment. Elagolix has no registered medicine in CIMA. [[ref:aemps-2026-ryeqo-yselty]]
items.pearl: With an agonist, add-back protects bone without reducing pain relief.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 18: strong, ⊕⊕; rec. 19 and 22: GPP; rec. 20: strong, ⊕⊕⊕; rec. 21: weak, ⊕⊕⊕ (moderate quality, but a weak recommendation because of uncertainty about dose, duration and add-back). NICE NG73 1.4.7 and 1.9.8 (links to TA1057 and TA1067 added September 2025); 1.9.5 [2017].

items.title: Refractory pain: aromatase inhibitors as the last medical step
items.core: For pain refractory to other medical or surgical treatment, ESHRE recommends aromatase inhibitors, which can be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists or antagonists (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE NG73 contains no recommendations on aromatase inhibitors. [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
The evidence is a 2011 systematic review, mostly of non-randomised studies and case reports, plus two later studies; long-term data are lacking. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Their side effects are mainly hypoestrogenic (vaginal dryness, hot flushes, reduced bone mineral density), so ESHRE reserves them for when all other medical or surgical options have been exhausted. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Because they are also used for ovulation induction, pregnancy, with higher rates of multiples, is a potential complication. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] In some countries they are not available, even off-label. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: For which patients does ESHRE reserve aromatase inhibitors, and what are they combined with?
items.pearl: Aromatase inhibitor for pain: only when everything else has failed, with the option of combining it with another hormone treatment, and with contraception in mind.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 23: strong, ⊕⊕ (based on a 2011 review of mostly non-randomised studies). NICE NG73: no recommendation on this drug class.

items.title: Surgery for pain and prevention of recurrence
items.core: ESHRE recommends offering surgery as one of the options to reduce pain (strong, ⊕⊕), suggests considering excision rather than ablation (weak, ⊕⊕) and asks for the choice between hormone treatment and surgery to be a shared decision (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] After surgery, it recommends considering a 52-mg levonorgestrel IUS or a combined hormonal contraceptive for at least 18–24 months for secondary prevention of dysmenorrhoea (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE suggests considering hormonal treatment after excision or ablation, for example with the combined pill, to prolong the benefits of surgery (1.9.7). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
For endometrioma, ESHRE recommends cystectomy rather than drainage and electrocoagulation for secondary prevention of pain, taking the risk to ovarian reserve into account (strong, ⊕⊕), followed by long-term hormone treatment if pregnancy is not sought immediately (strong, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Hysterectomy with removal of all visible lesions can be considered if pregnancy is no longer wanted and more conservative treatments have failed, explaining that it will not necessarily cure the symptoms or the disease (weak, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] For recurrent pain, any hormone treatment or surgery can be offered (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Where the guidelines differ: ESHRE does not recommend preoperative hormone treatment to improve the immediate outcome of surgery for pain (strong, ⊕⊕), whereas NICE suggests considering 3 months of GnRH agonist before surgery for deep endometriosis involving the bowel, bladder or ureter (1.9.5). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Which two hormonal options, and for how long, does ESHRE recommend after surgery to prevent recurrence of dysmenorrhoea?
items.pearl: If she is not seeking pregnancy, hormonal suppression follows surgery: ESHRE recommends it to prevent recurrence.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 24: strong, ⊕⊕; rec. 25: weak, ⊕⊕; rec. 37: GPP; rec. 64 and 65: strong, ⊕⊕; rec. 66: strong, ⊕; rec. 32: weak, ⊕⊕; rec. 69: weak, ⊕; rec. 35: strong, ⊕⊕. NICE NG73 1.9.5 and 1.9.7 [2017] (in 2017, off-label use for some drugs).

items.stem: Which of these statements about hormone treatment for endometriosis-associated pain is correct according to ESHRE?

options.text: Dienogest is superior to combined contraceptives and should always be the first choice.
options.why: ESHRE describes a similar magnitude of effect across hormone treatments, with none that must always come first, and asks for a shared decision (GPP).

options.text: All reduce pain similarly compared with placebo, and the choice depends on preferences, side effects, individual efficacy, cost and availability.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE describes a similar effect size across treatments and recommends shared decision-making (GPP).

options.text: The combined contraceptive is useful only in a cyclical regimen, never continuously.
options.why: ESHRE allows the combined pill to be offered continuously for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕⊕); according to a meta-analysis of a few small studies, continuous use may be superior for recurrence of dysmenorrhoea.

options.text: The levonorgestrel IUS has no role in endometriosis-associated pain.
options.why: ESHRE recommends the levonorgestrel IUS or etonogestrel implant to reduce pain (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

items.explanation: There is no winning hormone treatment: it is chosen to fit each woman and changed if it does not work or is not tolerated.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman (fictional case) not wishing to conceive still has pain despite a continuous combined contraceptive and, later, a progestogen. A GnRH agonist is being considered. What is most appropriate according to ESHRE?

options.text: GnRH agonist with combined hormonal add-back to prevent bone loss and hypoestrogenic symptoms.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE places agonists as second line after contraceptives or progestogens (GPP) and recommends considering add-back (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

options.text: Agonist without add-back, because add-back reduces pain relief.
options.why: In a meta-analysis of 13 trials, add-back improved lumbar bone density with no significant difference in dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia; ESHRE recommends it (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

options.text: An aromatase inhibitor alone as the next step.
options.why: ESHRE reserves aromatase inhibitors for pain refractory to other medical or surgical treatment; they may be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens, or GnRH agonists or antagonists (strong, ⊕⊕).

options.text: Oral danazol, given its long track record.
options.why: ESHRE no longer describes it as a pain treatment because of its severe side effects.

items.explanation: GnRH agonists and antagonists are second line after contraceptives or progestogens; with agonists, add-back protects bone without reducing efficacy.

items.stem: A woman with deep endometriosis involving the bowel is scheduled for surgery for pain. A trainee asks whether hormone treatment beforehand is advisable. Which answer best reflects the guidelines?

options.text: Both guidelines recommend 3 months of GnRH agonist before any endometriosis surgery.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend preoperative hormone treatment to improve the immediate outcome (strong, ⊕⊕), and NICE suggests it only for deep disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter (1.9.5).

options.text: ESHRE does not recommend preoperative hormone treatment to improve the surgical outcome, whereas NICE suggests considering 3 months of agonist for deep disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter.
options.why: Correct: this is a genuine disagreement between guidelines (ESHRE rec. 35, strong, ⊕⊕; NICE 1.9.5 [2017]).

options.text: Neither guideline addresses preoperative treatment.
options.why: Both address it: ESHRE against it to improve the immediate outcome, and NICE in favour of considering it for deep disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter.

options.text: NICE advises against preoperative agonist and ESHRE recommends it.
options.why: It is the other way round: NICE suggests considering it for deep disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter (1.9.5) and ESHRE does not recommend it (strong, ⊕⊕).

items.explanation: Faced with this disagreement, it helps to know both positions and decide with the patient and surgical team; the ESHRE recommendation is more recent (2022) and the NICE one dates from 2017.

items.stem: After removal of a 5-cm endometrioma for pain, a 32-year-old woman (fictional case) does not want a pregnancy for the next few years. What does ESHRE recommend to prevent recurrence?

options.text: No treatment: cystectomy alone already prevents recurrence.
options.why: ESHRE recommends long-term hormone treatment after endometrioma surgery if pregnancy is not sought immediately (strong, ⊕).

options.text: Long-term hormone treatment, for example a combined contraceptive or a 52-mg levonorgestrel IUS for at least 18–24 months.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE recommends long-term hormone treatment after endometrioma surgery (strong, ⊕) and considering the 52-mg IUS or combined contraceptive for at least 18–24 months to prevent dysmenorrhoea (strong, ⊕⊕).

options.text: 3 months of GnRH agonist and then nothing.
options.why: For secondary prevention, ESHRE recommends long-term hormone treatment, not a short course.

options.text: Schedule repeat surgery after 1 year.
options.why: ESHRE does not propose scheduled surgery; if pain recurs, any hormone treatment or surgery can be offered (weak, ⊕).

items.explanation: If she is not seeking pregnancy, endometrioma surgery is followed by long-term hormonal suppression to reduce recurrence of the cyst and of pain.

items.title: Non-medical strategies: discuss them without overpromising
items.core: ESHRE recommends discussing non-medical strategies for quality of life and psychological well-being, but cannot recommend any specific intervention (Chinese medicine, nutrition, electrotherapy, acupuncture, physiotherapy, exercise or psychological interventions) to reduce pain or improve quality of life, because the benefits and harms are unclear (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE states that the evidence does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other Chinese herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
Use is widespread: in a survey in Switzerland, Austria and Germany, 62.5% of patients used complementary and alternative medicine, with more use linked to dissatisfaction with healthcare, and another study describes at least 70% using heat, diet, meditation, breathing, non-prescribed drugs and alcohol. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Even so, there are very few studies on their efficacy and safety, and ESHRE calls for well-designed trials. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

NICE likewise found no high-quality research on diet, exercise or other non-medical treatments for pain, fatigue and other symptoms, frames this as a research question, and stresses that supporting self-management is critical to quality of life. [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Which non-medical interventions does ESHRE list as having no possible recommendation for pain and quality of life?
items.pearl: Asking what the patient already uses is part of the consultation: many do, and evidence of efficacy is scarce.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 38: GPP; research recommendation R11. NICE NG73 1.8.1 [2017] and research recommendation 3 (lifestyle interventions).

items.title: Diet and supplements for pain: omega-3, vitamin D and the specific diet that does not exist
items.core: ESHRE cannot recommend nutrition to improve pain or quality of life: the studies are small and lack proper controls, and there is not yet evidence to develop a specific endometriosis diet. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE states that the evidence does not support supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
Reviews summarised by ESHRE describe less pain with omega-3 fatty acids in small studies; in a small trial of vitamin D, fish oil and placebo, pain improved with vitamin D but similarly with placebo, and the improvement with fish oil was more modest. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Antioxidants, gluten and soy are poorly studied. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Based on a few studies, ESHRE notes in its text that fish oils might be suggested as an alternative to more harmful anti-inflammatories. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Women with endometriosis often change their diet because of symptoms, which complicates interpreting the studies: in one, they had more food intolerances (25.6% vs 7.7%) and gastrointestinal symptoms (77% vs 29%) than controls, and the authors suggested that input from a nutrition professional might help. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about a specific endometriosis diet, and what does it mention as a possible alternative to anti-inflammatories?
items.pearl: If the patient wants to try omega-3, it should not replace effective treatment or be presented as a treatment for the disease.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, sections II.6.e–f and rec. 38: GPP (no recommendation for nutrition); the fish oil mention is in the text, not a numbered recommendation. NICE NG73 1.8.1 [2017]. Nuance between guidelines: NICE supports no supplement; ESHRE leaves fish oil open as an alternative to more harmful anti-inflammatories.

items.title: Acupuncture, TENS, physiotherapy and exercise: what is known
items.core: ESHRE concludes that it cannot make recommendations on acupuncture, electrotherapy (including TENS), physiotherapy or exercise to reduce pain or improve quality of life in endometriosis. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
Acupuncture: the studies are small, non-specific and unblinded, with different types of acupuncture and no valid inert placebo. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Electrotherapy: there are 3 small studies with favourable results (TENS, neuromuscular electrical stimulation and laser), whose conclusions should be viewed with caution because of their design. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Physiotherapy: the evidence in pelvic pain is very poor and one review concluded that trigger point manual therapy cannot be recommended for chronic pain; pelvic floor training exists for urinary or bowel dysfunction that may accompany endometriosis, although there are no studies specific to it. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Exercise: in dysmenorrhoea in general (not specific to endometriosis), a Cochrane review with low-quality evidence suggests that exercise at least 3 times a week for about 45–60 minutes may reduce menstrual pain by around 25 mm on a 100-mm scale. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] ESHRE cannot recommend it for endometriosis for lack of studies, but considers it part of a healthy lifestyle. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: What exercise pattern and what effect on menstrual pain does the Cochrane review cited by ESHRE describe, and why does it not apply directly to endometriosis?
items.pearl: Having no recommendation does not make something harmful: exercise has general benefits, but it should not be presented as a treatment for endometriosis.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, sections II.6.a–c and rec. 38: GPP. The 25-mm figure comes from a Cochrane review on dysmenorrhoea in general, with low-quality evidence.

items.title: Psychological support and a multidisciplinary approach to pain
items.core: ESHRE cannot recommend a specific psychological intervention for pain or quality of life, because the studies are of low quality and heterogeneous, but it stresses awareness of the psychological impact of living with pain, infertility and functional pelvic problems, and considering access to psychological support. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE points out that endometriosis can be a long-term condition with physical, sexual, psychological and social impact, and may need long-term support (1.2.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
In a moderate-quality trial, psychotherapy with somatosensory stimulation improved pain and quality of life at 3 months compared with a waiting list, with improvement maintained at 6 and 24 months. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] ESHRE suggests considering follow-up and psychological support in confirmed endometriosis, particularly deep and ovarian disease (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] ESHRE considers it reasonable to draw on what is known in chronic pelvic pain, where the EAU guideline strongly recommends a multidisciplinary approach, and to offer options addressing psychological, sexual and physical factors to improve quality of life even when pain cannot be reduced. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

NICE asks that gynaecology services have access to a multidisciplinary pain management service (1.1.3), that information and support needs be assessed, including psychosexual and emotional needs (1.2.2), and that information be given on local support groups, online forums and national charities (1.2.3). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Which service does NICE say gynaecology services should have access to, and what support information should the patient be given?
items.pearl: Even if pain does not fully go away, quality of life can improve: addressing psychological, sexual and physical factors is part of treatment.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, section II.6.d and rec. 38: GPP; rec. 8: weak, ⊕. NICE NG73 1.1.3, 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 [2017]; 1.2.3 [2017, amended 2024].

items.stem: A patient with endometriosis (fictional case) asks whether a gluten-free diet with vitamin D and omega-3 can replace her contraceptive for pain control. Which answer fits the guidelines?

options.text: Yes: ESHRE recommends a specific anti-inflammatory diet for endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE concludes there is not yet evidence to develop a specific endometriosis diet and makes no recommendation on nutrition (GPP).

options.text: It cannot replace it: neither ESHRE nor NICE supports diet or supplements as treatment; ESHRE only mentions fish oil as a possible alternative to more harmful anti-inflammatories.
options.why: Correct: NICE states the evidence does not support supplements (1.8.1) and ESHRE cannot recommend nutrition; the fish oil mention is a comment in the text, not a numbered recommendation.

options.text: Yes, because vitamin D reduced pain more than placebo in a trial.
options.why: In the trial cited by ESHRE, the improvement with vitamin D was similar to that with placebo.

options.text: Yes, because the gluten-free diet is well studied in endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE notes that antioxidants, gluten and soy are poorly studied.

items.explanation: Diet and supplements can be discussed, but they do not replace a treatment with proven efficacy for pain.

items.stem: Which of these statements about non-medical interventions for endometriosis-associated pain is correct according to ESHRE?

options.text: Acupuncture has a strong recommendation because several meta-analyses show benefit.
options.why: ESHRE makes no recommendation on acupuncture: although there are several meta-analyses, the studies they summarise are small, non-specific and unblinded, and no valid inert placebo exists.

options.text: TENS is recommended as first line, before NSAIDs.
options.why: ESHRE cannot make recommendations on electrotherapy, which rests on 3 small studies to be interpreted with caution.

options.text: No specific non-medical intervention can be recommended, although non-medical strategies for quality of life and psychological well-being should be discussed.
options.why: Correct: this is ESHRE recommendation 38 (GPP).

options.text: Exercise is discouraged because it worsens pain.
options.why: ESHRE does not discourage it: it considers exercise part of a healthy lifestyle and cites low-quality evidence of less menstrual pain with exercise in dysmenorrhoea in general.

items.explanation: No recommendation does not mean forbidden: options are discussed honestly about the lack of evidence, without delaying effective treatment.

items.title: Case: Nuria and the pain that was not “normal”

steps.text: Nuria (fictional case), 27, presents with severe dysmenorrhoea since adolescence, dyschezia during periods and deep dyspareunia; she misses 1–2 days of work a month. She does not want to become pregnant. Her sister has endometriosis. NICE asks clinicians to suspect endometriosis with these symptoms and to ask about first-degree relatives (1.3.1, 1.3.2). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

Pelvic examination and transvaginal ultrasound are normal. ESHRE points out that negative imaging does not exclude endometriosis, particularly superficial peritoneal disease, and NICE asks not to exclude it in this situation (1.5.4). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

An NSAID and a continuous combined pill are prescribed, which ESHRE allows to be offered for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] She is told that hormonal treatment reduces pain and has no permanent negative effect on her fertility (1.4.5). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

After 3 months the pain has improved only partly. Nuria has read on social media about a gluten-free diet, vitamin D and omega-3, and asks whether she could stop the pill. Neither ESHRE nor NICE supports diet or supplements as treatment for endometriosis. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

After switching to a progestogen, the pain still limits her daily life and she is referred to gynaecology, as NICE advises when initial treatment is not effective or symptoms affect daily living (1.5.5). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] There, two routes are discussed: laparoscopy to diagnose and treat, which ESHRE suggests considering when imaging is negative or empirical treatment has failed (GPP) and which NICE considers even if the ultrasound was normal (1.5.11), or a GnRH agonist with add-back as second-line medical treatment. Nuria prefers to avoid surgery for now, and the agonist is chosen. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

Nuria also asks about acupuncture and exercise. It is explained that ESHRE cannot recommend any specific non-medical intervention but does recommend discussing strategies for her quality of life and psychological well-being (GPP), and she is given information on support groups and access to a multidisciplinary pain service, as NICE suggests (1.1.3, 1.2.3). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

items.stem: ESHRE summarises a study in a UK primary care database: the odds of an endometriosis diagnosis rose with the number of symptoms (OR 5.0 with 1 symptom and 84.7 with 7). Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: 84.7% of women with 7 symptoms have endometriosis, so with 7 symptoms the diagnosis is practically made.
options.why: It confuses an odds ratio with a probability: 84.7 is not a percentage of affected women.

options.text: With a single symptom the probability of endometriosis is 5%, so an isolated symptom allows it to be ruled out.
options.why: Again it confuses the OR with a probability, and ESHRE does not use these data to rule out the disease.

options.text: They are odds ratios: the odds of diagnosis rise with more symptoms, although symptoms alone predict weakly.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE describes the predictive ability of symptoms as weak and incomplete, but increasing with their number.

options.text: They show that symptoms are enough for diagnosis, so ESHRE no longer considers imaging necessary.
options.why: ESHRE states the opposite: symptoms alone predict the disease weakly and incompletely.

items.explanation: An odds ratio compares odds; it does not express the percentage of women with the disease. ESHRE uses this study to show that the likelihood of diagnosis rises with the number of symptoms, although the ability of symptoms alone to predict endometriosis is weak and incomplete.

items.stem: According to the context section of NICE NG73, what delay can occur between a woman first reporting symptoms and confirmation of endometriosis?

options.text: 4 to 10 years, partly because the importance of symptoms goes unrecognised.
options.why: Correct: this is the figure and the explanation in NICE’s context section.

options.text: 6 to 12 months, mainly because of waiting lists for laparoscopy in public hospitals.
options.why: Figure and cause invented: NICE describes 4 to 10 years and cites failure to recognise the symptoms.

options.text: 15 to 20 years, because the disease almost never causes symptoms until infertility appears.
options.why: Invented figure, and endometriosis causes symptoms such as dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia before infertility.

options.text: 1 to 2 years, a delay NICE considers acceptable because it does not change the prognosis of the disease.
options.why: Invented figure, and NICE does not present the delay as acceptable.

items.explanation: NICE describes that delays of 4 to 10 years can occur between first reporting symptoms and confirmation of the diagnosis. Patient groups note that clinicians often do not recognise the importance of symptoms and that women may delay seeking help because they perceive pelvic pain as normal. The figure comes from the guideline’s context, not from a recommendation.

items.stem: A patient with severe dysmenorrhoea asks whether keeping a pain diary is of any use. Which best reflects what NICE NG73 and ESHRE say?

options.text: NICE advises against it because it delays diagnosis; ESHRE strongly recommends it because it shortens time to diagnosis.
options.why: NICE asks clinicians to say that a diary helps the discussion, and ESHRE acknowledges there is no evidence it shortens diagnosis.

options.text: Both consider it essential to diagnose endometriosis without the need for imaging or physical examination.
options.why: Neither presents it as a diagnostic tool replacing examination or imaging.

options.text: NICE says it aids the discussion; ESHRE says it complements history taking, though there is no evidence it shortens diagnosis.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.3.3 and an ungraded statement of ESHRE’s guideline development group.

options.text: Neither mentions it; only validated apps have solid evidence that they reduce diagnostic delay in endometriosis.
options.why: Both mention it, and ESHRE finds no evidence that diaries, questionnaires or apps shorten diagnosis.

items.explanation: NICE advises telling women that a pain and symptom diary can aid discussions (1.3.3). ESHRE acknowledges there is no evidence that a diary, questionnaire or app shortens time to diagnosis, but considers that they complement history taking because they help objectify pain.

items.stem: In a prospective study of 129 women summarised by ESHRE, clinical examination for rectosigmoid involvement had a sensitivity of 39% and a specificity of 97%. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: A normal examination safely rules out rectosigmoid involvement, because specificity is very high.
options.why: Ruling out depends on sensitivity, which is low: a normal examination misses many lesions.

options.text: The examination detects 97% of rectosigmoid lesions and gives false positives in 39% of cases.
options.why: It reverses the terms: 39% is the sensitivity (lesions detected) and 97% is the specificity.

options.text: With these figures the examination is so accurate that ESHRE considers ultrasound unnecessary for the rectum.
options.why: ESHRE notes that transvaginal ultrasound was superior for the rectosigmoid and recommends considering imaging even if the examination is normal.

options.text: A normal examination misses many lesions, whereas false positives are uncommon.
options.why: Correct: low sensitivity (39%) and high specificity (97%).

items.explanation: Sensitivity indicates what proportion of lesions the examination detects (39%); specificity, what proportion of women without a lesion the examination identifies as normal (97%). That is why a normal examination does not close the work-up: ESHRE recommends (strong, ⊕⊕) considering further diagnostic steps, including imaging, even if the examination is normal.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman (fictional case) with suspected endometriosis and a history of sexual abuse declines vaginal examination. What is appropriate according to ESHRE and NICE?

options.text: Insist on vaginal examination, because ESHRE considers it essential before ordering any imaging.
options.why: ESHRE notes that in these cases vaginal examination should ideally be omitted and other techniques used first.

options.text: Omit it, offer an abdominal examination to exclude masses and use other techniques, such as imaging, first.
options.why: Correct: it combines the ESHRE position and NICE 1.3.6.

options.text: Order a CA-125 instead, because it replaces examination when the patient declines it.
options.why: Neither source proposes CA-125 as a substitute for examination; in adolescents ESHRE recommends not using it to diagnose or rule out.

options.text: Rule out endometriosis, since without a pelvic examination, normal or abnormal, the suspicion cannot be sustained.
options.why: Suspicion also rests on symptoms, and ESHRE recommends considering further diagnostic steps, including imaging, even when the examination is inconclusive.

items.explanation: ESHRE warns that vaginal or rectovaginal examination may be inappropriate or very painful, for example in adolescents, for religious reasons or after sexual abuse, and that in those cases it should ideally be omitted and other techniques used first. If pelvic examination is declined or not suitable, NICE offers an abdominal examination to exclude masses (1.3.6).

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman (fictional case) with dysmenorrhoea that stops her working has an ultrasound appointment in 6 weeks. According to NICE NG73, what should be done about drug treatment?

options.text: Wait for the ultrasound, because NICE asks for endometriosis to be confirmed before starting any treatment.
options.why: NICE asks for the opposite: ultrasound and referral in parallel with initial treatment.

options.text: Wait for the specialist assessment, because NICE reserves treatment for the endometriosis specialist.
options.why: NICE does not reserve initial treatment for the specialist; it starts it while the work-up is completed.

options.text: Start initial drug treatment now, in parallel with the ultrasound and, if needed, referral.
options.why: Correct: this is what NICE 1.5.1 recommends.

options.text: Start only a GnRH agonist, because the response serves as a diagnostic test before the ultrasound.
options.why: NICE does not propose agonists as a diagnostic test; in NG73 they appear only as an adjunct before surgery for deep disease.

items.explanation: NICE advises carrying out ultrasound and, if needed, referral in parallel with initial drug treatment (1.5.1). ESHRE agrees on trying to relieve symptoms, either empirically or after a diagnosis.

items.stem: On the role of laparoscopy in diagnosing endometriosis, which sentence best reflects the difference in emphasis between ESHRE and NICE?

options.text: ESHRE questions the “dogma” of laparoscopy as the gold standard; NICE’s context section still presents it as the only route to a definitive diagnosis.
options.why: Correct: this is the difference in emphasis between the two guidelines.

options.text: ESHRE requires laparoscopy before any treatment; NICE has completely replaced it with ultrasound and MRI.
options.why: ESHRE accepts empirical treatment without laparoscopy, and NICE recommends considering laparoscopy even if imaging is normal.

options.text: Both advise against diagnostic laparoscopy because of its morbidity and reserve it for removing endometriomas larger than 3 cm.
options.why: Neither advises against it: ESHRE proposes it if imaging is negative or empirical treatment fails, and NICE considers it even with normal imaging.

options.text: NICE questions laparoscopy as the gold standard; ESHRE keeps it as the only route to a definitive diagnosis.
options.why: It reverses the positions: it is ESHRE that questions the gold standard and NICE’s context that keeps laparoscopy as the only route.

items.explanation: ESHRE questions the “dogma” of laparoscopy as the gold standard because it is invasive with potential morbidity, and proposes offering it if imaging is negative or empirical treatment was unsuccessful or inappropriate (GPP). NICE’s context still describes it as the only route to a definitive diagnosis, and NICE recommends considering it even if ultrasound or MRI was normal (1.5.11).

items.stem: Deep endometriosis is suspected in a 34-year-old woman (fictional case) who is going to have surgery. According to NICE NG73, what is advisable before operative laparoscopy?

options.text: Serial CA-125, to stage the disease and decide the extent of bowel resection.
options.why: NICE does not propose CA-125 to stage disease or plan surgery.

options.text: A separate prior diagnostic laparoscopy, to confirm the disease before operating.
options.why: NICE does not propose a prior diagnostic laparoscopy: it suggests considering a specialist ultrasound or MRI before the operative one.

options.text: Choose treatment according to the stage shown on imaging, rather than by symptoms and preferences.
options.why: NICE asks for treatment to be guided by the woman’s symptoms, preferences and priorities, not by stage (1.6.1).

options.text: A specialist ultrasound or MRI, to plan surgery for the deep disease.
options.why: Correct: this is what NICE 1.5.12 suggests considering when deep disease is suspected.

items.explanation: If deep endometriosis is suspected, NICE suggests considering a specialist ultrasound or MRI before operative laparoscopy (1.5.12). It also asks for treatment to be offered according to the woman’s symptoms, preferences and priorities rather than the stage (1.6.1).

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman (fictional case) with confirmed endometriosis and two 4-cm endometriomas decides not to have surgery. According to NICE NG73, what follow-up should be considered?

options.text: None, because NICE only proposes outpatient follow-up for women who have already had surgery for their endometriomas.
options.why: NICE proposes follow-up particularly for those who choose not to have surgery.

options.text: Outpatient follow-up, with or without examination and pelvic imaging, as she has endometriomas larger than 3 cm.
options.why: Correct: this is one of the situations in NICE 1.7.1.

options.text: MRI every 3 months indefinitely, because NICE requires it to detect malignant change early.
options.why: NICE sets no such schedule, and ESHRE notes there is no evidence that monitoring detects malignancy earlier.

options.text: Definitive discharge, because endometriomas under 5 cm need no surveillance at all according to NICE.
options.why: NICE’s threshold for considering follow-up is an endometrioma larger than 3 cm; the 5-cm figure is invented.

items.explanation: NICE suggests considering outpatient follow-up, with or without examination and pelvic imaging, in confirmed endometriosis, particularly when the woman chooses not to have surgery, if there is deep disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter, or 1 or more endometriomas larger than 3 cm (1.7.1).

items.stem: According to ESHRE, what is known about regular follow-up of women with confirmed endometriosis?

options.text: A six-monthly ultrasound is strongly recommended, because it has been shown to detect malignancy earlier.
options.why: ESHRE notes there is no evidence that monitoring detects recurrence, complications or malignancy earlier.

options.text: No follow-up should be done, because ESHRE advises against it for lack of evidence of benefit.
options.why: ESHRE does not advise against it: it suggests considering it (weak, ⊕), especially in deep and ovarian disease.

options.text: It is recommended only in adolescents, with an annual CA-125 as a marker of disease recurrence.
options.why: ESHRE does not limit it to adolescents or propose CA-125, which in adolescents it recommends not using to diagnose.

options.text: It may be considered, especially in deep and ovarian disease, with individualised frequency.
options.why: Correct: weak, ⊕, with individualised frequency as a GPP, although there is no evidence it detects problems earlier.

items.explanation: ESHRE suggests considering follow-up and psychological support in confirmed endometriosis, particularly deep and ovarian disease (weak, ⊕), although there is no evidence that regular monitoring detects recurrence, complications or malignancy earlier, and asks for its frequency to be individualised (GPP).

items.stem: According to NICE NG73, which of these resources should a specialist endometriosis service have access to?

options.text: A gynaecological oncology service that reviews every patient before any endometriosis surgery.
options.why: It is not on the NICE 1.1.4 list.

options.text: An in-house laboratory to measure CA-125 serially in every patient under follow-up for deep endometriosis.
options.why: It is not on the NICE 1.1.4 list, which mentions advanced diagnostic facilities such as radiology and histopathology.

options.text: A colorectal surgeon and a urologist with an interest in endometriosis, and a multidisciplinary pain service.
options.why: Correct: they are on the NICE 1.1.4 list, together with other resources.

options.text: A paediatric intensive care unit to care for young women aged 17 and under.
options.why: It is not on the list; for young women aged 17 and under NICE proposes a paediatric and adolescent gynaecology service or a specialist centre.

items.explanation: For NICE, the specialist service should have access to gynaecologists with advanced laparoscopic skills, a colorectal surgeon and a urologist with an interest in endometriosis, a specialist nurse, a multidisciplinary pain service with expertise in pelvic pain, a professional with expertise in gynaecological imaging of endometriosis, advanced diagnostic facilities and fertility services (1.1.4).

items.stem: In an adolescent with dysmenorrhoea, which risk factors for endometriosis does ESHRE recommend looking for in the history?

options.text: Family history, obstructive genital malformations, early menarche or short cycles.
options.why: Correct: this is ESHRE’s list (strong, ⊕).

options.text: Late menarche, long cycles and a family history of polycystic ovary syndrome.
options.why: ESHRE cites early menarche and short cycles, not late menarche or long cycles.

options.text: A raised serum CA-125, overweight and early onset of sexual activity.
options.why: ESHRE recommends not using CA-125 in adolescents, and the other factors are not on its list.

options.text: Only the intensity of menstrual pain, because other personal and family history items add no useful information.
options.why: ESHRE expressly recommends looking for several risk factors in the history.

items.explanation: In adolescents, ESHRE recommends careful history taking for risk factors: family history, obstructive genital malformations, early menarche or short cycles (strong, ⊕). It also suggests considering endometriosis with cyclical school absenteeism or use of oral contraceptives for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕).

items.stem: In a 14-year-old girl (fictional case) with suspected endometriosis, transvaginal ultrasound is not appropriate. According to ESHRE, what is appropriate?

options.text: Order CA-125: if normal, endometriosis is ruled out and no imaging is needed.
options.why: ESHRE recommends not using serum biomarkers such as CA-125 to diagnose or rule out (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

options.text: Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy straight away, without first trying any other imaging technique.
options.why: ESHRE proposes alternative imaging; laparoscopy may be considered if imaging is negative and NSAIDs or contraceptives have failed.

options.text: Consider MRI or transabdominal, transperineal or transrectal ultrasound, without using CA-125.
options.why: Correct: strong, ⊕⊕, for alternative imaging and strong, ⊕⊕⊕, for not using CA-125.

options.text: Do no tests until she turns 18, because imaging is unreliable before that age.
options.why: ESHRE sets no such age: it recommends imaging adapted to the adolescent’s situation.

items.explanation: In adolescents, ESHRE recommends transvaginal ultrasound where appropriate and, if not, considering MRI or transabdominal, transperineal or transrectal ultrasound (strong, ⊕⊕). It recommends not using serum biomarkers such as CA-125 to diagnose or rule out endometriosis (strong, ⊕⊕⊕).

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl (fictional case) with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis still has pain despite hormonal contraceptives and a progestogen. Which is correct about GnRH agonists according to ESHRE?

options.text: They are contraindicated under age 18, so the only remaining option is radical surgery.
options.why: ESHRE does not contraindicate them in adolescents: it considers them in this situation, with conditions.

options.text: They can be used without time limit and without add-back, because at this age bone mass recovers by itself.
options.why: ESHRE limits them to 1 year and with add-back.

options.text: They should be the first hormonal step in adolescents, before contraceptives or progestogens.
options.why: In adolescents ESHRE recommends hormonal contraceptives or progestogens as first line.

options.text: For up to 1 year, with add-back and after discussion in secondary or tertiary care.
options.why: Correct: weak, ⊕⊕, with the specialist discussion as a GPP.

items.explanation: In adolescents, ESHRE reserves GnRH agonists for laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis after hormonal contraceptives or progestogens have failed, for up to 1 year and with add-back (weak, ⊕⊕), and only after discussion with a secondary or tertiary care practitioner (GPP). NICE refers young women aged 17 and under to paediatric and adolescent gynaecology or a specialist centre.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman (fictional case) with suspected endometriosis has taken naproxen and paracetamol for 3 months without enough relief. According to NICE NG73, what comes next?

options.text: Continue the same analgesics for 12 more months, because NICE sets one year as the minimum trial length.
options.why: NICE gives a trial of about 3 months as an example, not a year.

options.text: Consider other forms of pain management and referral for further assessment.
options.why: Correct: this is what NICE 1.4.3 proposes if relief is inadequate.

options.text: Move straight to an aromatase inhibitor, which NICE recommends as the second step.
options.why: NICE NG73 contains no recommendations on aromatase inhibitors.

options.text: Add a strong opioid indefinitely, which NICE considers the usual next step.
options.why: NICE NG73 does not mention opioids; it proposes considering other forms of pain management and referral.

items.explanation: NICE suggests considering a short trial (for example, 3 months) of paracetamol or an NSAID, alone or in combination, as first line (1.4.2) and, if relief is inadequate, considering other forms of pain management and referral for further assessment (1.4.3).

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman (fictional case) with endometriosis is trying to conceive and takes an NSAID daily throughout the cycle. According to ESHRE, what is relevant?

options.text: There is some limited evidence that NSAIDs taken continuously through the cycle might inhibit ovulation.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE mentions it because of its relevance when pregnancy is sought.

options.text: NSAIDs slow the progression of endometriosis, so they should be taken daily while trying to conceive.
options.why: ESHRE states there is no evidence that analgesics affect disease progression.

options.text: The evidence for NSAIDs in endometriosis comes from several large high-quality trials, with no effect on ovulation.
options.why: The evidence is limited to one small, very-low-quality trial, and ESHRE mentions a possible effect on ovulation.

options.text: NSAIDs are contraindicated in endometriosis because of their gastrointestinal effects, whatever the wish for pregnancy.
options.why: ESHRE states they may be offered (weak, ⊕); it mentions gastrointestinal effects as a side effect, not a contraindication.

items.explanation: ESHRE states that NSAIDs or other analgesics may be offered to reduce pain (weak, ⊕). Their evidence is limited to one small, very-low-quality trial, there is no evidence they affect progression, they can cause gastrointestinal side effects, and there is some limited evidence that continuous use through the cycle might inhibit ovulation.

items.stem: In a woman with endometriosis-associated pain, a neuromodulator (a tricyclic antidepressant, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin) is being considered. What do the sources report?

options.text: ESHRE strongly recommends them as first line, ahead of NSAIDs and hormone treatment.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend them as first line; it describes that they have not shown clear superiority over placebo.

options.text: In chronic pelvic pain trials they have not been clearly superior to placebo; NICE refers to its neuropathic pain guideline.
options.why: Correct: this is how ESHRE summarises it, and NICE 1.4.4 refers to that guideline.

options.text: NICE expressly advises against them in endometriosis because of their severe, dose-limiting side effects.
options.why: NICE does not advise against them: it refers to its neuropathic pain guideline for their use.

options.text: They have been shown to slow lesion progression, so they are recommended before surgery.
options.why: Neither source attributes an effect on progression to them or recommends them before surgery.

items.explanation: Neuromodulators are used for chronic pain, but in chronic pelvic pain trials they have not been clearly superior to placebo and sometimes cause severe, dose-limiting side effects. NICE refers to its neuropathic pain guideline for their use (1.4.4).

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman (fictional case) with endometriosis does not want to take the combined pill because she fears it will harm her future fertility. According to NICE NG73, what do you explain?

options.text: That hormone treatment reduces pain and has no permanent negative effect on subsequent fertility.
options.why: Correct: this is what NICE asks clinicians to explain (1.4.5).

options.text: That she is right: NICE recommends avoiding hormone treatment in those who wish to conceive in the future.
options.why: NICE does not recommend this; it explains there is no permanent negative effect on subsequent fertility.

options.text: That the effect on fertility is permanent, but worthwhile because treatment cures endometriosis.
options.why: NICE explains there is no permanent negative effect, and does not present hormone treatment as curative.

options.text: That only surgery improves pain without affecting fertility, so it should always be the first treatment option.
options.why: NICE offers hormone treatment for suspected, confirmed or recurrent endometriosis; surgery is not the only option.

items.explanation: NICE offers hormone treatment, for example the combined pill or a progestogen, for suspected, confirmed or recurrent endometriosis (1.4.6), and asks clinicians to explain that it reduces pain and has no permanent negative effect on subsequent fertility (1.4.5).

items.stem: With what strength and quality of evidence does ESHRE allow the combined pill to be offered continuously for endometriosis-associated dysmenorrhoea?

options.text: Strong recommendation with high-quality evidence (⊕⊕⊕⊕), with no need to discuss breakthrough bleeding.
options.why: The recommendation is weak with low-quality evidence, and ESHRE asks for possible breakthrough bleeding to be discussed.

options.text: Strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence (⊕), only in adolescents who do not tolerate cyclical use.
options.why: Neither the strength, the quality nor the population match ESHRE’s for this recommendation.

options.text: It does not allow it: ESHRE only accepts cyclical use, because continuous use lacks studies in endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE does allow continuous use for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕⊕).

options.text: Weak recommendation with low-quality evidence (⊕⊕), discussing possible breakthrough bleeding.
options.why: Correct: this is how it appears in ESHRE 2022.

items.explanation: ESHRE recommends the combined hormonal contraceptive as a pill, ring or patch for dyspareunia, dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pain (strong, ⊕⊕), and allows the combined pill to be offered continuously for dysmenorrhoea (weak, ⊕⊕), discussing possible breakthrough bleeding. Strength and quality of evidence are different things.

items.stem: A patient is about to start dienogest for endometriosis. According to the long-term studies summarised by ESHRE, which fact is correct?

options.text: They used 20 mg/day, and the most frequent side effect in one of them was weight gain, in 7%.
options.why: Invented dose and figure: the studies used 2 mg/day and the most frequent effect was vaginal bleeding (71.9%).

options.text: They used 2 mg/day, and described no vaginal bleeding because dienogest produces complete amenorrhoea.
options.why: The dose is correct, but in one of them vaginal bleeding was the most frequent side effect.

options.text: They used 2 mg/day, and in one of them vaginal bleeding was the most frequent side effect (71.9%).
options.why: Correct: these are the data ESHRE summarises.

options.text: They showed that dienogest reduces pain far more than any other available hormone treatment.
options.why: ESHRE describes all hormone treatments as reducing pain by a similar magnitude compared with placebo.

items.explanation: ESHRE recommends progestogens (strong, ⊕⊕), taking their different side-effect profiles into account (GPP). The long-term dienogest studies it summarises used 2 mg/day, and in one vaginal bleeding was the most frequent side effect (71.9%). It is worth anticipating this when prescribing.

items.stem: ESHRE grades oral GnRH antagonists for pain as “weak, ⊕⊕⊕”. What explains this combination?

options.text: It is an error in the guideline: with moderate evidence, the recommendation would by definition have to be strong.
options.why: Strength and quality of evidence are different things; moderate evidence can accompany a weak recommendation.

options.text: The evidence is very low, but the group recommends them strongly because of their oral convenience over agonists.
options.why: It reverses the terms: ⊕⊕⊕ is moderate evidence and the recommendation is weak.

options.text: Moderate evidence, but a weak recommendation because of uncertainty about dose, duration and need for add-back.
options.why: Correct: this is the justification ESHRE gives.

options.text: Moderate evidence and a weak recommendation because antagonists do not reduce pain more than placebo.
options.why: ESHRE does not say they fail to beat placebo: it recommends considering them for their effect, with uncertainties about their use.

items.explanation: On ESHRE’s GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕ is moderate evidence. Even so, the recommendation to consider oral GnRH antagonists is weak because of uncertainty about dose, duration and need for add-back, and they are placed as second line (GPP).

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman (fictional case) in Spain has endometriosis pain despite previous medical and surgical treatment. Which oral GnRH antagonist has no registered medicine in CIMA?

options.text: Relugolix with estradiol and norethisterone acetate (Ryeqo), authorised only for fibroids in Spain.
options.why: Ryeqo is authorised and marketed in Spain for symptomatic endometriosis after previous treatment.

options.text: Linzagolix (Yselty), authorised in the EU, but not registered in Spain for any indication.
options.why: Yselty is authorised and marketed in Spain for symptomatic endometriosis after previous treatment.

options.text: All three are authorised and marketed in Spain for symptomatic endometriosis.
options.why: Elagolix has no registered medicine in CIMA.

options.text: Elagolix, whose trials ESHRE summarises, but which has no registered medicine in CIMA.
options.why: Correct: Ryeqo and Yselty are authorised and marketed in Spain.

items.explanation: In Spain, relugolix with estradiol and norethisterone acetate (Ryeqo) and linzagolix (Yselty) are authorised and marketed for symptomatic endometriosis after previous medical or surgical treatment. Elagolix, whose trials ESHRE summarises, has no registered medicine in CIMA.

items.stem: Which sentence best describes the place of GnRH-acting drugs in NICE NG73 compared with ESHRE?

options.text: NICE recommends agonists as first line for pain; ESHRE reserves them for the preoperative period.
options.why: It is the other way round: ESHRE recommends them for pain as second line, and in NICE they appear only before surgery for deep disease.

options.text: In NICE, agonists appear only before surgery for deep disease, and for antagonists it points to its technology appraisals.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.9.5 for agonists and 1.4.7 and 1.9.8 (TA1057 and TA1067) for antagonists.

options.text: NICE advises against oral antagonists for lack of data; ESHRE strongly recommends them as first line.
options.why: NICE points to technology appraisals that cover them, and ESHRE suggests considering them (weak) as second line.

options.text: Both guidelines recommend agonists without add-back for a maximum of 3 months in any clinical situation.
options.why: ESHRE recommends considering add-back with agonists, and NICE’s 3 months refer only to the preoperative period for deep disease.

items.explanation: ESHRE recommends GnRH agonists for pain as second line, with add-back, and suggests considering oral antagonists. In NICE NG73, agonists appear only as an adjunct before surgery for deep disease (1.9.5), and for antagonists it points to its technology appraisals in adults of reproductive age after medical or surgical treatment: linzagolix with add-back (TA1067) and relugolix–estradiol–norethisterone (TA1057).

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman (fictional case) with endometriosis pain refractory to all medical and surgical treatments is about to start an aromatase inhibitor. According to ESHRE, what must be taken into account?

options.text: That pregnancy, with more multiples, is a potential complication.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE notes it as a potential complication, because these drugs are used to induce ovulation.
