options.text: That it must always be used without any other hormone treatment, because combinations cancel its effect.
options.why: ESHRE states it can be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists or antagonists.

options.text: That it has no hypoestrogenic effects, so bone mass need not be monitored during treatment.
options.why: Its side effects are mainly hypoestrogenic, including reduced bone mineral density.

options.text: That there are solid long-term data from large randomised trials supporting its safety over years.
options.why: The evidence is a 2011 review, mostly of non-randomised studies, and long-term data are lacking.

items.explanation: For pain refractory to other treatments, ESHRE recommends aromatase inhibitors, which can be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists or antagonists (strong, ⊕⊕). Their side effects are mainly hypoestrogenic, long-term data are lacking and, because they are used to induce ovulation, pregnancy, with higher rates of multiples, is a potential complication.

items.stem: On aromatase inhibitors for refractory endometriosis pain, which sentence correctly reflects the two guidelines?

options.text: ESHRE recommends them for refractory pain (strong, ⊕⊕); NICE NG73 contains no recommendations on them.
options.why: Correct: NICE not addressing them is not the same as advising against them.

options.text: ESHRE recommends them for refractory pain (strong, ⊕⊕); NICE NG73 expressly advises against them.
options.why: NICE NG73 does not advise against them: it simply contains no recommendations on them.

options.text: Both recommend them as second line, right after contraceptives and before agonists.
options.why: ESHRE reserves them for when the other options are exhausted, and NICE does not address them.

options.text: ESHRE recommends them with high-quality evidence (⊕⊕⊕⊕) from randomised trials; NICE proposes them in adolescents.
options.why: ESHRE’s evidence is low (⊕⊕) and mostly non-randomised, and NICE does not address them.

items.explanation: ESHRE recommends aromatase inhibitors for pain refractory to other medical or surgical treatment (strong, ⊕⊕), based mainly on a 2011 review of non-randomised studies, and reserves them for when the other options are exhausted. NICE NG73 contains no recommendations on this drug class.

items.stem: In endometriosis surgery for pain, what does ESHRE propose about technique and about endometriomas?

options.text: Ablation rather than excision, and drainage with electrocoagulation of the endometrioma to protect ovarian reserve.
options.why: It reverses both proposals: ESHRE prefers excision and cystectomy.

options.text: Excision or ablation interchangeably, and no surgical treatment of an endometrioma under 5 cm.
options.why: ESHRE suggests considering excision, and the 5-cm threshold is invented.

options.text: Excision rather than ablation, and cystectomy rather than drainage with electrocoagulation, weighing ovarian reserve.
options.why: Correct: excision, weak, ⊕⊕; cystectomy, strong, ⊕⊕.

options.text: Hysterectomy from the outset in every woman with an endometrioma, because it guarantees definitive cure of symptoms and disease.
options.why: ESHRE reserves hysterectomy for specific cases and warns that it does not necessarily cure symptoms or disease.

items.explanation: ESHRE suggests considering excision rather than ablation (weak, ⊕⊕). For endometrioma it recommends cystectomy rather than drainage and electrocoagulation for secondary prevention of pain, taking the risk to ovarian reserve into account (strong, ⊕⊕), followed by long-term hormone treatment if pregnancy is not sought immediately.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman (fictional case) with endometriosis, not wishing to conceive and with failed conservative treatments, asks for a hysterectomy. According to ESHRE, which is correct?

options.text: It is discouraged in endometriosis, because ESHRE considers it never improves pain.
options.why: ESHRE does not discourage it: it can be considered in this situation (weak, ⊕⊕).

options.text: It can be considered, removing all visible lesions and explaining that it will not necessarily cure the symptoms or disease.
options.why: Correct: weak, ⊕⊕, in women not wishing to conceive after more conservative treatments have failed.

options.text: It is the first-line option for every woman over 40, with a strong recommendation and high-quality evidence.
options.why: ESHRE considers it after conservative options have failed, with a weak recommendation.

options.text: It guarantees cure if done without removing the lesions, because removing the uterus is enough.
options.why: ESHRE refers to removing all visible lesions and warns that it does not necessarily cure.

items.explanation: ESHRE suggests considering hysterectomy with removal of all visible lesions when pregnancy is no longer wanted and more conservative treatments have failed, explaining that it will not necessarily cure the symptoms or the disease (weak, ⊕⊕). For recurrent pain, any hormone treatment or surgery can be offered (weak, ⊕).

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (fictional case), operated on for peritoneal endometriosis because of pain, does not want a pregnancy for the next 3 years. What reflects the guidelines on preventing recurrence of dysmenorrhoea?

options.text: ESHRE proposes a GnRH agonist for 3 months after surgery and then no treatment.
options.why: ESHRE proposes a 52-mg levonorgestrel IUS or a combined contraceptive for at least 18–24 months.

options.text: Neither guideline proposes postoperative treatment, because surgery alone prevents recurrence.
options.why: Both propose hormone treatment after surgery.

options.text: NICE requires repeat laparoscopy at one year to confirm there is no recurrence before starting treatment.
options.why: NICE does not propose a check laparoscopy; it suggests considering hormone treatment after surgery.

options.text: ESHRE recommends considering a 52-mg levonorgestrel IUS or a combined contraceptive for at least 18–24 months; NICE, hormone treatment.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE (strong, ⊕⊕) and NICE 1.9.7, for example with the combined pill.

items.explanation: After surgery, ESHRE recommends considering a 52-mg levonorgestrel IUS or a combined hormonal contraceptive for at least 18–24 months for secondary prevention of dysmenorrhoea (strong, ⊕⊕). NICE suggests considering hormone treatment after excision or ablation, for example with the combined pill, to prolong the benefits of surgery (1.9.7).

items.stem: A patient with endometriosis asks whether Chinese herbs can treat her disease. Which answer reflects the guidelines?

options.text: NICE says the evidence does not support Chinese medicine to treat it; ESHRE cannot recommend it, but asks for non-medical strategies to be discussed.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.8.1 and ESHRE recommendation 38 (GPP).

options.text: Both guidelines recommend it as a first-line complement because it improves pain in quality trials.
options.why: Neither recommends it: NICE says the evidence does not support it and ESHRE cannot recommend it.

options.text: ESHRE strongly advises against it because of proven harms, and NICE recommends it only in adolescents.
options.why: ESHRE cannot recommend it because benefits and harms are unclear, and NICE recommends it in no group.

options.text: Neither guideline mentions it, so there is no reason to discuss non-medical therapies with the patient.
options.why: Both mention it, and ESHRE recommends discussing non-medical strategies for quality of life.

items.explanation: NICE states that the evidence does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other Chinese herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1). ESHRE recommends discussing non-medical strategies for quality of life and psychological well-being, but cannot recommend any specific intervention because benefits and harms are unclear (GPP).

items.stem: In a survey in Switzerland, Austria and Germany summarised by ESHRE, what proportion of patients with endometriosis used complementary and alternative medicine, and what was greater use linked to?

options.text: 12.5%, and greater use was linked to milder disease and less pain.
options.why: Invented figure and association: it was 62.5%, linked to dissatisfaction with healthcare.

options.text: 95%, and greater use was linked to having had a laparoscopic diagnosis.
options.why: Invented figure and association: it was 62.5%, linked to dissatisfaction with healthcare.

options.text: 62.5%, and greater use was linked to a university level of education.
options.why: The figure is right, but the association described is with dissatisfaction with healthcare.

options.text: 62.5%, and greater use was linked to dissatisfaction with healthcare.
options.why: Correct: this is the finding ESHRE summarises.

items.explanation: Use of non-medical therapies is widespread: in that survey, 62.5% used complementary and alternative medicine, more so with greater dissatisfaction with healthcare. Even so, there are very few studies on their efficacy and safety, so it is worth asking what each patient uses.

items.stem: According to a study summarised by ESHRE, what was the difference between women with endometriosis and controls in food intolerances and gastrointestinal symptoms?

options.text: More intolerances (25.6% vs 7.7%) and gastrointestinal symptoms (77% vs 29%) with endometriosis.
options.why: Correct: the authors suggested that input from a nutrition professional might help.

options.text: Fewer intolerances (7.7% vs 25.6%) and fewer gastrointestinal symptoms (29% vs 77%) than the control group.
options.why: It reverses the groups: the higher figures belonged to women with endometriosis.

options.text: No difference, which shows that diet has no influence at all on endometriosis symptoms.
options.why: There were clear differences, and the study does not allow concluding that diet has no influence.

options.text: More intolerances, which led ESHRE to recommend a specific gluten-free diet for endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE states there is not yet evidence for a specific diet, and gluten is poorly studied.

items.explanation: Women with endometriosis often change their diet because of symptoms, which complicates interpreting the studies. In one, they had more food intolerances (25.6% vs 7.7%) and gastrointestinal symptoms (77% vs 29%) than controls, and the authors suggested input from a nutrition professional. ESHRE still cannot recommend a specific diet.

items.stem: How should ESHRE’s mention of fish oils in endometriosis be understood, and how does it compare with NICE?

options.text: It is a strong numbered ESHRE recommendation, and NICE also recommends omega-3 as a supplement.
options.why: It is not a numbered recommendation, and NICE states that the evidence does not support supplements.

options.text: ESHRE expressly advises against omega-3 because of bleeding risk, and NICE allows it as treatment.
options.why: ESHRE does not advise against it, and NICE supports no supplement for treating endometriosis.

options.text: It is a suggestion in the text, based on a few studies, as an alternative to more harmful anti-inflammatories; NICE does not support supplements.
options.why: Correct: this is the nuance between the two guidelines.

options.text: It is an ESHRE recommendation to replace hormone treatment with omega-3 and vitamin D in mild endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE does not propose replacing hormone treatment; in one trial, the improvement with vitamin D was similar to placebo.

items.explanation: ESHRE cannot recommend nutrition for pain, but in its text, based on a few studies, it notes that fish oils might be suggested as an alternative to more harmful anti-inflammatories; this is not a numbered recommendation. NICE states that the evidence does not support supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1).

items.stem: A patient with endometriosis asks whether exercise will relieve her menstrual pain. What does the Cochrane review cited by ESHRE describe?

options.text: In endometriosis, 20 minutes a day halves pain, with high-quality evidence.
options.why: Invented regimen, effect and quality; the review concerns dysmenorrhoea in general and its evidence is low quality.

options.text: In dysmenorrhoea in general, exercise at least 3 times a week for about 45–60 minutes may reduce pain by about 25 mm on a 100-mm scale.
options.why: Correct: low-quality evidence and not specific to endometriosis.

options.text: In endometriosis, exercise worsens pain, so ESHRE advises against it during menstruation.
options.why: ESHRE does not advise against it: it considers it part of a healthy lifestyle.

options.text: In dysmenorrhoea in general, daily exercise reduces pain more than NSAIDs, with moderate-quality evidence.
options.why: The review does not compare with NSAIDs in those terms, and its evidence is low quality.

items.explanation: A Cochrane review on dysmenorrhoea in general, with low-quality evidence, suggests that exercise at least 3 times a week for about 45–60 minutes may reduce menstrual pain by around 25 mm on a 100-mm scale. ESHRE cannot recommend it for endometriosis for lack of studies, but considers it part of a healthy lifestyle.

items.stem: According to ESHRE, why can it make no recommendations on acupuncture and electrotherapy for endometriosis pain?

options.text: Because large, well-blinded trials showed that both are ineffective compared with placebo.
options.why: There are no large, well-blinded trials: the problem is the weakness of the studies, not proven ineffectiveness.

options.text: Because both are contraindicated in endometriosis owing to the risk of stimulating lesions.
options.why: ESHRE does not contraindicate them or mention that risk.

options.text: Because they have only been studied in adolescents, and the results cannot be extrapolated to adult women.
options.why: ESHRE does not describe that limitation; it describes small studies with design problems.

options.text: Acupuncture studies small and unblinded, with no valid inert placebo; for electrotherapy, 3 small studies to be viewed with caution.
options.why: Correct: this is how ESHRE summarises it.

items.explanation: ESHRE describes acupuncture studies as small, non-specific and unblinded, with different types of acupuncture and no valid inert placebo. For electrotherapy there are 3 small studies with favourable results (TENS, neuromuscular electrical stimulation and laser), whose conclusions should be viewed with caution because of their design. That is why it cannot make recommendations.

items.stem: According to NICE NG73, what should services caring for women with endometriosis offer or have in terms of support?

options.text: Psychological support only during the first month after diagnosis, because it is usually not needed afterwards.
options.why: NICE points out that it can be a long-term condition that may need long-term support.

options.text: Mandatory psychiatric referral of every woman with chronic pain before any treatment.
options.why: NICE does not propose such mandatory referral; it asks for needs to be assessed and access to a pain service.

options.text: Access to a multidisciplinary pain service, assessment of psychosexual and emotional needs and information on support groups.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.1.3, 1.2.2 and 1.2.3.

options.text: Information only through the hospital website, because NICE advises against forums and patient associations.
options.why: NICE asks for information on local support groups, online forums and national charities.

items.explanation: NICE asks that gynaecology services have access to a multidisciplinary pain management service (1.1.3), that information and support needs be assessed, including psychosexual and emotional needs (1.2.2), and that information be given on local support groups, online forums and national charities (1.2.3). It notes that endometriosis may need long-term support (1.2.1).

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman (fictional case) with deep endometriosis still has pain despite optimal treatment. Which best reflects ESHRE’s position on psychological support?

options.text: It cannot recommend a specific intervention, but asks for access to psychological support to be considered and psychological, sexual and physical factors addressed.
options.why: Correct: even when pain cannot be reduced, this approach can improve quality of life.

options.text: ESHRE strongly recommends a specific psychotherapy because several high-quality trials show it cures pain.
options.why: ESHRE cannot recommend a specific psychological intervention: the studies are low quality and heterogeneous.

options.text: Psychological support only makes sense once pain disappears, so treatment success must be awaited first.
options.why: ESHRE proposes offering options to improve quality of life even when pain cannot be reduced.

options.text: ESHRE advises against psychological support in deep endometriosis because it distracts from surgical treatment.
options.why: It is the other way round: it suggests considering follow-up and psychological support particularly in deep and ovarian disease (weak, ⊕).

items.explanation: ESHRE cannot recommend a specific psychological intervention because of the low quality and heterogeneity of the studies, although in a moderate-quality trial psychotherapy with somatosensory stimulation improved pain and quality of life compared with a waiting list. It suggests considering follow-up and psychological support, particularly in deep and ovarian disease (weak, ⊕), and, as in chronic pelvic pain, addressing psychological, sexual and physical factors even when pain cannot be reduced.

aemps-2026-ryeqo-yselty.title: Fichas técnicas de Ryeqo 40 mg/1 mg/0,5 mg (relugolix/estradiol/acetato de noretisterona) e Yselty 100 y 200 mg (linzagolix)
aemps-2026-ryeqo-yselty.authors: AEMPS, CIMA; EMA (autorización centralizada); titulares Gedeon Richter y Theramex
aemps-2026-ryeqo-yselty.population: Adult women of reproductive age with symptomatic fibroids or endometriosis (Spain/EU).
aemps-2026-ryeqo-yselty.finding: Both are authorised and marketed in Spain for moderate to severe fibroid symptoms and for symptomatic treatment of endometriosis in women with previous medical or surgical treatment. Initial EU authorisation: Ryeqo 16 July 2021, Yselty 14 June 2022 (the date of the endometriosis indication was not verified). There is no elagolix medicine in CIMA.

eshre-2022-endometriosis.title: ESHRE guideline: endometriosis (full guideline)
eshre-2022-endometriosis.authors: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline Development Group (Becker CM, Bokor A, Heikinheimo O, Horne A, Jansen F, Kiesel L, King K, Kvaskoff M, Nap A, Petersen K, et al.)
eshre-2022-endometriosis.population: Women with diagnosed or strongly suspected endometriosis; includes chapters on pain, infertility, recurrence, adolescence and menopause. Does not cover adenomyosis. Literature search up to 1 Dec 2020. Full 192-page guideline; recommendations labelled strong or weak (GRADE) with their level of evidence (⊕ symbols), plus good practice points (GPP) and guideline group (GDG) statements.
eshre-2022-endometriosis.finding: Diagnosis: use imaging (ultrasound or MRI), aware that a negative result does not exclude it, particularly superficial peritoneal disease (rec. 5, strong, ⊕⊕); do not use biomarkers (rec. 4, strong, ⊕⊕⊕); diagnostic laparoscopy or imaging plus empirical treatment, with no proven superiority of either (GDG statement); empirical treatment is considered if the patient is not trying to conceive. Infertility: do not prescribe ovarian suppression to improve fertility (rec. 39, strong, ⊕⊕) or postoperative suppression solely to enhance pregnancy rates (rec. 40, strong, ⊕⊕); operative laparoscopy in rASRM stage I/II (rec. 43, weak, ⊕⊕); for endometrioma (rec. 44, weak, ⊕) and deep disease (rec. 45, weak, ⊕); use the EFI to identify who benefits from ART after surgery (GDG statement); IUI with ovarian stimulation in stage I/II (rec. 47, weak, ⊕); ART if tubal or male factor, low EFI or failed other treatments (rec. 49, weak, ⊕⊕); no preferred protocol (rec. 50, weak, ⊕); no extended GnRH agonist before ART (rec. 53, strong, ⊕); insufficient evidence for COC/progestogen pre-treatment (rec. 54, weak, ⊕); no routine surgery before ART in stage I/II (rec. 55, strong, ⊕⊕) or for endometrioma (rec. 56, strong, ⊕⊕); endometrioma surgery before ART for pain or follicle access (rec. 57, GPP); fertility preservation: discuss pros and cons with extensive ovarian endometriosis (rec. 59, strong, ⊕); no non-medical intervention (nutrition, Chinese medicine, acupuncture, etc.) can be recommended to increase fertility (GDG statement).
eshre-2022-endometriosis.limitations: Read in the full guideline: the list of recommendations (pp. 9–14), sections I.2.b–I.2.c, II.3.e (ovarian reserve) and III.1–III.8. The guideline produced no GRADE summary-of-findings tables because evidence was insufficient; most infertility recommendations rest on ⊕ or ⊕⊕ evidence and several are GPPs (expert opinion). Level of evidence per Annex 4: ⊕ very low, ⊕⊕ low, ⊕⊕⊕ moderate, ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high; a recommendation can be strong with ⊕ evidence. Surgical studies were not stratified by EFI. Search closed in 2020; whether a later update exists was not checked.

nice-2024-ng73.title: Endometriosis: diagnosis and management (NG73)
nice-2024-ng73.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2024-ng73.population: Women and people with suspected or confirmed endometriosis, including those aged 17 and under, in the English health system. Published 6 Sep 2017; last updated 11 Nov 2024. Each recommendation carries the year it was written or changed ([2017], [2024], [2017, amended 2024]); NICE does not attach GRADE grades in the recommendation text.
nice-2024-ng73.finding: Offer transvaginal ultrasound to anyone with suspected endometriosis even if examination is normal (1.5.2); do not exclude endometriosis if examination and ultrasound are normal (1.5.4); do not use CA125 to diagnose it (1.5.8); consider specialist ultrasound or MRI for deep disease (1.5.9) and laparoscopy even if imaging is normal (1.5.11); refer to a specialist centre for endometrioma or deep disease (1.5.6); treat according to symptoms, preferences and priorities rather than stage (1.6.1). When fertility is a priority: offer excision or ablation plus adhesiolysis for disease not involving bowel, bladder or ureter (1.10.1); offer laparoscopic cystectomy or drainage and ablation of endometriomas, taking into account that drainage and ablation may preserve ovarian reserve more (1.10.2); discuss benefits and risks of surgery for deep endometriosis (1.10.3); do not offer hormonal treatment alone or with surgery to people trying to conceive (1.10.4). Does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1).
nice-2024-ng73.limitations: Read sections 1.5–1.10, the rationale for 1.10.2–1.10.4 and the context (full PDF, 33 pp.). The fertility recommendations are to be read alongside NICE NG257; the evidence on hormonal treatment combined with surgery is described as mixed. Evidence reviews A and B were not read. Guideline designed for the English health system.
